details:
Project Name

NovaRoute: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

High-Level Project Summary

NovaRoute is a free browser game, with no download and no account, in which kids aged about 7 to 12 command a crewed outpost on the Moon or Mars. In Outpost Command, a real-time builder, they explore a dark map with a rover, place buildings on ice and ore, give six crew their jobs and plan the crew's day the way NASA plans a space station's: work, meals, exercise, calls home and sleep. Power, air, water, food, radiation and the crew's mood all pull against each other, so every choice is a trade-off with no single right answer. Solar storms follow the real Sun: today's flares from NASA's DONKI space-weather database set how hard a storm hits, so a shielding decision depends on current space weather. Buildings wear out, level up and break in meteoroid strikes and dust storms, and the mission is won by fuelling the rocket home with oxygen and water made on site. Every number is rounded from NASA data and credited in the game. It matters because children learn why missions succeed by trying, failing safely and playing again.

Link to Project Demo

https://nubispace.nubicode.com/pitch

(A seven-slide deck, title slide included: team, member, challenge, the problem, what students do, how the trade-offs are tested, the NASA data that makes it possible, the classroom, and what comes next.)

Link to Final Project

https://nubispace.nubicode.com

The same site is also at https://main.d313un6zdjexzz.amplifyapp.com.

Detailed Project Description

What it does. NovaRoute is a mission trainer built around one idea from the challenge: a real outpost lives or dies by trade-offs. It has three ways to play the same trade-offs, an academy, and a teacher guide.

  • Outpost Command (/command/moon, /command/mars): a real-time outpost builder. Six crew land at Shackleton crater's rim (Moon) or Arcadia Planitia (Mars) with a hub, one solar array and a few sols of supplies. The map is mostly dark until a scout rover explores it. Players place 14 kinds of building (solar arrays, batteries, oxygen plant, ice drill, metal mine, greenhouse, lab, habitat, reactor, water recycler, storm shelter, workshop, comms dish, launch pad), assign crew, research six upgrades and grow the landing site through three eras into a base. They win by fuelling the ascent vehicle with oxygen, water and food made on site (living off the land, or ISRU).
    • Power decides everything else. Solar arrays make nothing in the Moon's two-sol dark or at night on Mars, and little in a dust storm; a reactor works all the time. The game forecasts when the battery runs dry and whether storage will last the next dark, and players can switch buildings off.
    • A real crew day. The crew keep a 24-hour clock like a space station crew: up at 06:00, three 30-minute meals, planning calls with Earth morning and evening, work, at least an hour of exercise, free time and 8.5 hours of sleep, with a rest day each week. A Schedule tab is the calendar. Crew only work in work hours; more work makes more, but too little sleep, exercise, contact with home or rest lowers mood, and tired crews make more mistakes. Skipping exercise lowers fitness, as bone and muscle weaken in low gravity.
    • Things wear out. Every building has a condition bar: it wears down (faster outside in the dust), takes damage from meteoroid strikes and moonquakes, and breaks at zero until free crew repair it. Buildings can be upgraded to level II and III as the outpost grows.
    • Surprises with choices. Fourteen kinds of situation (breakdowns, meteoroid strikes, air leaks, dust storms, moonquakes, the radio blackout when Mars is behind the Sun, ice and ore finds, supply drops, homesickness, illness and more) stop the clock and ask the player to choose. Each ends with a real NASA fact. Solar flares arrive with a warning; the shelter alarm and a storm shelter keep the dose under NASA's 30-day limit of 250 mSv.
    • Built to be understood. A pinned status bar shows every supply and how fast it changes, a "Next step" line always says what to do now, a day-and-night strip shows the light cycle, warnings float over the map, and a how-to-play guide opens on the first game. Every building, upgrade, research option and schedule choice explains itself with a short real fact. A Demo button lets mission control play while the player watches, and a map code gives a whole class the same map.
  • Quick drill (/mission/moon, /mission/mars): the first fifteen sols of Outpost Command, about four minutes, with its own stars.
  • Classroom edition (/classic/moon, /classic/mars): the turn-based version. Pack a 6-tonne (Moon) or 7-tonne (Mars) lander, then plan ten turns of power and crew jobs against scripted events, with prediction questions and a debrief naming the one limit that decided the mission. A Moon mission takes about 20 minutes and Mars about 30, so it fits a lesson.
  • Astronaut Academy (/learn): sixteen short stations in five levels, from how NASA picks astronauts and what space does to the body, through the ISS, Earth, the Sun, the Moon, asteroids, Mars and other stars, to commanding a Mars expedition (the Senior level is labelled for ages 12 and up). Each station has a short article in four lessons, live NASA data to explore, a prediction, recall cards and a five-question quiz generated from that data and scored on the server. A Solar System Explorer shows where planets, spacecraft, asteroids and comets are today from NASA JPL data.
  • For teachers (/teachers): objectives, NGSS 3-5-ETS1-1 to 3 (grades 3 to 5) and MS-ETS1-1 to 4 (grades 6 to 8) alignment, a 45-minute lesson plan, discussion questions, the sources behind every number, and what the model simplifies.

Everything that teaches is public. An account (a username, a nickname and a password, no email) is only needed to keep progress across devices.

How it works. Outpost Command's simulation is pure and seeded: a seed and a list of choices always replay to the same outpost, so classes can compare runs fairly, and all randomness (the map, situations, rover finds) comes from the seed. It advances an hour at a time: power first, then crew work by the schedule, supplies, building and repairs, wear, radiation and mood. NASA DONKI is fetched on the server once an hour; if it cannot be reached, a saved copy is shown and labelled "saved", never "live". 749 automated tests check the game, including bots that play whole missions: a careful commander keeps the outpost alive on every map, on both worlds and under quiet, typical and active Suns, and often flies home; a commander who does nothing always fails. They also check that solar-only Moon bases freeze in the dark, that Mars without a recycler runs dry, and that staying outside in a storm passes the radiation limit.

Benefits and what we hope to achieve. Students learn mass and power budgets, margins, redundancy, shielding, crew health and in-situ resources by doing, failing safely (nobody is hurt: crew who cannot be kept safe are flown home) and playing again. It runs on school laptops and phones with nothing to install. We hope teachers use it as a one-lesson activity and that children leave knowing why a Moon or Mars base is hard, and that they could help solve it.

Honest limits. The brief suggests two or three core resources; the classroom edition keeps to that, while Outpost Command shows nine readings because it is the deeper game. The site is in English only. The Open Science Data Repository is not used.

Tools. TypeScript, Next.js 15, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, next-intl, Jest and Testing Library, hosted on AWS Amplify, with Amazon Cognito and DynamoDB for optional accounts. Built on the design and teaching system of NubiCode's AlFred learning platform.
